blocks.text: Except beryllium, Group 2 metals react with water to form metal hydroxides, M(OH)2, and hydrogen gas. Beryllium does not react with water or steam, even when heated, because of its protective oxide layer.

blocks.caption: Reactions with water
rows: cold water: more vigorous than Mg

blocks.alt: A beaker of water with a lump of calcium at the bottom giving off a stream of hydrogen bubbles; the water is turning cloudy. The equation Ca + 2H2O gives Ca(OH)2 + H2 is written above, and a note says the cloudiness is sparingly soluble calcium hydroxide.
blocks.caption: Calcium reacting with cold water (original diagram after Figure 17.3).
blocks.long_description: Calcium reacts with cold water more vigorously than magnesium, producing hydrogen gas and calcium hydroxide: Ca(s) + 2H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2 + H2(g). Because calcium hydroxide is only sparingly soluble, some of it separates as a white precipitate, making the water cloudy.

blocks.text: Calcium hydroxide is sparingly soluble and forms a white precipitate. Group 2 hydroxides are less basic than Group 1 hydroxides, but their basic character increases down the group as their solubility increases.
